## Statement

Let $I=[a,b]$ with $a<b$, let $e:I\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, and let
$E=\|e\|_{\infty,I}>0$. Put
$S_+=\{x\in I:e(x)=E\}$ and $S_-=\{x\in I:e(x)=-E\}$. If there are no
$n+2$ increasing points of $S_+\cup S_-$ with alternating signs, then there
is a real polynomial $h$ of degree at most $n$ such that
$e(x)h(x)>0$ for every $x\in S_+\cup S_-$.

1.1 Continuity and attainment in [F2] show that $S_+\cup S_-$ is nonempty and compact: the maximum of $|e|$ is attained and $E>0$, while each level set is closed in the compact interval [F1]. If one of $S_+$ or $S_-$ is empty, take $h=1$ or $h=-1$ according to the sign of the nonempty set; this has degree zero and the required sign. [given, F1, F2, construct]

1.2 Suppose both sets are nonempty. Their product is a closed bounded subset of $\mathbb R^2$. For $(x,y),(x',y')\in\mathbb R^2$, the reverse and ordinary triangle inequalities in [F3] give $\bigl||x-y|-|x'-y'|\bigr|\le |(x-y)-(x'-y')|\le |x-x'|+|y-y'|\le2\|(x,y)-(x',y')\|_2$, so the distance function is continuous. By [F2] it attains a minimum separation $\delta=\min\{|x-y|:x\in S_+,\,y\in S_-\}$. This minimum is positive because a minimizing pair at distance zero would give a point in both disjoint sets. Starting at the leftmost point of $S_+\cup S_-$, repeatedly take the first point of the opposite-sign set to the right and the last current-sign point before it. These extrema exist because the level sets are compact, and each transition gives an open gap of length at least $\delta$ containing no point of $S_+\cup S_-$. The process therefore has finitely many transitions, each with a distinct ordered gap. [given, F1, F2, F3, construct]

The extremal union cannot be empty by attainment of the positive supremum; either individual sign set can be empty and then a constant with the appropriate sign works.

$$\ell_j(x)=\prod_{\substack{0\le k\le n\\k\ne j}}\frac{x-c_k}{c_j-c_k},\qquad p(x)=\sum_{j=0}^n y_j\ell_j(x).$$
Then $p$ is the unique polynomial of degree at most $n$ satisfying $p(c_j)=y_j$. In particular, interpolation reproduces every polynomial of degree at most $n$.

1.1 Since $c_j-c_k

e m$, while every factor in $\ell_m(c_m)$ equals $1$; hence $\ell_j(c_m)=1$ exactly when $j=m$. The displayed $p$ has degree at most $n$ and $p(c_m)=y_m$. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 If $q$ is another such polynomial, then $q-p$ has degree at most $n$ and vanishes at the $n+1$ distinct nodes. ## Definition

On $\operatorname{Re}z>0$, define

$$\ell_+(z)=-\operatorname{Log}z-\gamma_Ez+ \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac zn-\operatorname{Log}\left(1+\frac zn\right)\right).$$

Here $\operatorname{Log}$ is the principal logarithm from
[[def-complex-logarithms-principal-logarithm-and-complex-powers]], and
$\gamma_E$ denotes Euler's constant $\gamma$ from
[[def-euler-mascheroni-constant]]. Both $z$ and $1+z/n$ lie in the
principal-logarithm domain. The local uniform convergence of this series
and the identity $e^{\ell_+(z)}=\Gamma(z)$ are established by
[[lem-loggamma-series-convergence-and-gamma-identity]].

## Definition

Let $S=[0,1]^2$ and let $T=\{(x,y):0\le y\le x\le1\}$ be the reference triangle. The **vertex Duffy map** is $D:S\to T$, $D(r,s)=(r,rs)$. Its image, inverse for $r>0$, and Jacobian determinant are verified in [[lem-duffy-reference-map-jacobian-and-image]]. The change-of-variables use and endpoint limit for weak singularities are proved in [[thm-duffy-weak-singularity-transform]].

## Definition

Write $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. For $m\in\mathbb N_0$ and $T\in\mathbb R$, define the finite-integral extension
$$F_m(T)=\int_0^1 t^{2m}\exp(-Tt^2)\,dt.$$
The **Boys function** is the restriction to the conventional domain $T\ge0$. The extension to negative $T$ is used only for ordinary center derivatives at the boundary value $T=0$; the finite evaluator below accepts no negative argument.
For $s>0$ and $T>0$, write the lower incomplete-gamma integral as
$$\gamma(s,T)=\int_0^T u^{s-1}\exp(-u)\,du.$$
The complete Euler Gamma function $\Gamma(s)$ has the existing meaning in [[def-euler-gamma-function]], namely $\Gamma(s)=\int_0^\infty u^{s-1}e^{-u}\,du$ for real $s>0$.

The integrand defining $F_m$ is continuous on $[0,1]$ and positive on $(0,1]$, so $F_m(T)$ exists, is positive, and, for $T\ge0$, satisfies $F_m(T)\le1/(2m+1)$. The index $m$ is an arbitrary nonnegative integer; no fixed maximum order is part of this definition.

## Statement

Assume AC. A nonempty bounded contractible Lipschitz polyhedron $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ has nonempty connected boundary. In particular the connected-boundary clause of the regular-decomposition theorem follows from the domain assumptions in the discrete-compactness theorem.

1.1 Put $M=\overline\Omega$. It is compact by boundedness and closedness. Near each boundary point a Lipschitz graph chart $x_3=\phi(x')$ straightens $M$ by the explicit homeomorphism $(x',x_3)\mapsto(x',x_3-\phi(x'))$ to a closed halfspace neighborhood. Interior points use Euclidean balls. These charts show that $M$ is a Hausdorff second-countable three-manifold with topological boundary exactly $\partial\Omega$ and interior exactly $\Omega$. Its orientation is the standard Euclidean orientation on its interior; this is precisely the orientation convention for manifolds with boundary in [F2]. By [F1], $\Omega\hookrightarrow M$ is a homotopy equivalence. Contractibility of $\Omega$, [F3], and factorization through a point give $H^2(M;\mathbb R)=0$: the point has one singular simplex in each degree, and its real cochain differentials are successively zero and identity, so its positive cohomology is zero. Also $M$ is path connected: its interior is path connected by contractibility, and a half-chart path joins any boundary point to its interior. The augmentation identifies $H_0(M;\mathbb R)$ with $\mathbb R$, because any difference of points is the boundary of a path and every zero-chain of coefficient sum zero is a finite linear combination of such differences. The boundary is nonempty: a ray from any interior point eventually leaves the bounded set and its first exit point is a boundary point. [F1, F3, construct, F2]

2.1 By [F2], $H_1(M,\partial M;\mathbb R)=0$. The exact sequence in [F3] then makes $H_0(\partial M;\mathbb R)\to H_0(M;\mathbb R)$ injective. The boundary is a two-manifold by the graph charts, hence locally path connected, so its connected components are path components. If there were two, choose one point in each. Their difference is nonzero in $H_0(\partial M;\mathbb R)$: the sum of coefficients on the first path component defines a linear functional on zero-chains which kills every one-simplex boundary, yet sends this difference to one. Its image in $H_0(M;\mathbb R)$ is zero since the two points are joined by a path in $M$, contradicting injectivity. Therefore the nonempty boundary is connected. No finite-element incidence matrix is used to infer this continuum topological claim. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the ultrafilter lemma, Dependent Choice and Hahn–Banach. Let
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open, $d\ge1$, and let
$1<p<\infty$. Then $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, with the norm inherited
from $W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, is a separable reflexive real Banach space.

1.2 Extend each $g\in L^p(\Omega)$ by zero to $\mathbb R^d$. This is an isometry into $L^p(\mathbb R^d)$ because $\Omega$ is measurable, and restriction of the rational box-step dense family in [F4] shows that $L^p(\Omega)$ is separable. Finite products of this countable dense family are countable and dense in $Y:=L^p(\Omega)^{d+1}$. The map $u\mapsto(u,\partial_1u,\ldots,\partial_du)$ embeds $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ isometrically into $Y$ by [F5]. Thus $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$, viewed as a subspace of $Y$, has a countable base obtained by intersecting it with the countable rational-ball base of $Y$. [A1, F4, F5, given, construct]

2.1 Choose one point from each nonempty member of that countable relative base, using Countable Choice [A1]. The chosen countable set meets every nonempty relatively open set, so it is dense in $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$. Together with step 1.1 this proves both assertions. [A1, F6, step 1.1, step 1.2, choose] ∎

## Statement

For $x\in[0,1]$, $g\in C([0,1],\mathbb R)$, and $0<\varepsilon<1$, let
$$S_{x,\varepsilon}(g):=\int_{[0,1]\setminus(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)}|x-y|^{-1/2}g(y)\,dy,$$
where the integral is the sum of the ordinary Riemann integrals on the at most
two remaining closed intervals, and an empty interval contributes zero. The
limit
$$S_x(g):=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}S_{x,\varepsilon}(g)$$
exists. The map $S_x:C([0,1],\mathbb R)\to\mathbb R$ is linear and positive, and its
operator norm ([[def-operator-norm]]) is
$$\|S_x\|=S_x(1)=2\sqrt{x}+2\sqrt{1-x}\le2\sqrt2.$$

1.1 By [F7], $M=\|g\|_\infty$ is finite. The integrand $y\mapsto |x-y|^{-1/2}g(y)$ is continuous on each closed interval in $[0,1]\setminus(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)$, because that set stays away from $x$. Thus the truncated integrals are finite and defined by [F1]. [given, F1, F2, F7]

## Statement

On the channel $\Omega=\mathbb T\times(0,1)$, with periodic coordinate
$x\in\mathbb T=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ and wall coordinate $y$, consider the
smooth tentative velocity
$$ \widetilde u(x,y)=(\cos(2\pi x)y(1-y),0). $$
The field need not be divergence-free; it is zero on both walls. Apply the
unit-step pressure projection that solves
$$ \Delta\phi=\nabla\cdot\widetilde u,\qquad \partial_y\phi(x,0)=\partial_y\phi(x,1)=0, $$
periodically in $x$, and sets $u=\widetilde u-\nabla\phi$. The corrected
normal velocity is zero at each wall, but its tangential velocity at $(0,0)$
is $-2\pi g(0)\ne0$, where
$$ g(0)=\frac{2\pi}{(2\pi)^4}\left(2\pi\coth\pi-2\right)>0. $$
Thus this pressure boundary condition does not preserve tangential no-slip
for this field. The example asserts no convergence rate.

1.1 Write $a=c=2\pi$. Direct differentiation gives $\nabla\cdot\widetilde u=-c\sin(ax)y(1-y)$. Define $$ g(y)=-\frac c{a^2}y^2+\frac c{a^2}y-\frac{2c}{a^4} +\frac{c}{a^3\sinh(a/2)}\cosh(a(y-1/2)),\qquad \phi(x,y)=\sin(ax)g(y). $$ Differentiating the polynomial and hyperbolic terms gives $g''-a^2g=-c y(1-y)$ and $g'(0)=g'(1)=0$. By [F2], this $\phi$ solves the stated Poisson problem and satisfies both Neumann conditions. Since $\widetilde u_y=0$ and $\partial_y\phi=0$ at the walls, the corrected normal velocity remains zero. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

## Definition

A compatible labeled initial mesh is a finite matching affine simplicial triangulation $\mathcal T_0$ of a polygon in $\mathbb R^2$ as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]; matching means distinct cell interiors are disjoint and any shared boundary is a complete common facet. with labels on its edges such that each triangle has one edge labeled $0$ and two labeled $1$, and every shared edge has the same label from both incident triangles. For a descendant triangle of generation $g(K)$, its three edge labels, in any order, are $(g(K)+1,g(K)+1,g(K))$. The unique edge labeled $g(K)$ is its reference edge.

To bisect $K$, join the midpoint of its reference edge to the opposite vertex. The two resulting triangles have generation $g(K)+1$. In each child, the two new half-edges and the bisector receive label $g(K)+2$; the one inherited nonreference edge retains label $g(K)+1$ and is the child's reference edge. A finite bisection forest is the collection of the initial triangles and all descendants reached by finitely many such bisections; its leaves form a triangulation when all shared-edge subdivisions agree. The admissible family $\mathbb T(\mathcal T_0)$ consists of the matching conforming leaf triangulations generated by these compatible bisections. A refinement $\mathcal T\le\mathcal T_*$ means every cell of $\mathcal T_*$ lies in a cell of $\mathcal T$.

The compatible initial labeling is a hypothesis, not a consequence of an arbitrary initial triangulation. This definition is two-dimensional and makes no claim about three-dimensional closure or complexity.

## Definition

Assume Countable Choice for the $L^2$ and Sobolev conventions of [[def-countable-choice]].

All functions and data are real-valued. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2$ be a bounded polygon and let $\mathcal T$ be a finite conforming matching triangulation by nondegenerate affine triangles, with maximum shape-regularity constant $\Gamma$. Write $h_K=\operatorname{diam}K$ and $h_E=\operatorname{diam}E$. Let $V(\mathcal T)$ be the continuous, piecewise-affine zero-boundary subspace of [[def-broken-and-conforming-polynomial-spaces]], which lies in $H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ by [[thm-matching-continuous-piecewise-polynomials-are-wkp]] and [[thm-zero-boundary-piecewise-polynomials-in-w10p]]. The exact weak model is
$$-\Delta u+b\cdot\nabla u=f,\qquad u\in H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R),\quad f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R),\quad b\in\mathbb R^2\ \text{constant}.$$
The weak form is $\int_\Omega\nabla u\cdot\nabla v+(b\cdot\nabla u)v\,dx=\int_\Omega fv\,dx$ for every $v\in H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R)$. The case $b=0$ is the symmetric Laplace model. Given $U\in V(\mathcal T)$, its cell residual is $R_K(U)=f|_K-b\cdot\nabla(U|_K)$; this is $f+\Delta U-b\cdot\nabla U$ because $\Delta U=0$ on each cell. For an interior edge $E=K^+\cap K^-$ define the outward flux jump
$$J_E(U)=\nabla U|_{K^+}\cdot n_{K^+}+\nabla U|_{K^-}\cdot n_{K^-},$$
where $n_{K^\pm}$ are the unit outward normals. Set
$$\eta_K(U)^2=h_K^2\|R_K(U)\|_{L^2(K)}^2+\frac12\sum_{E\subset\partial K,\ E\ {\rm interior}}h_E\|J_E(U)\|_{L^2(E)}^2,$$

## Definition

Assume [[def-countable-choice|Countable Choice]].

Let $\Omega^-$ be a nonempty bounded connected open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ whose boundary $\Gamma=\partial\Omega^-$ is a compact connected orientable Lipschitz surface. A **Lipschitz graph chart** is a rigid coordinate change in which $\Gamma$ is the graph $x_3=\psi(x_1,x_2)$ of a Lipschitz function on an open subset of $\mathbb R^2$, with $\Omega^-$ on one side of that graph. A **polyhedral boundary** is such a boundary made from finitely many planar polygonal faces meeting along edges and vertices; all surface-discretization claims below use this polyhedral subclass. Put $\Omega^+=\mathbb R^3\setminus\overline{\Omega^-}$ and assume $\Omega^+$ is connected. The unit normal $n$ points from $\Omega^-$ into $\Omega^+$ and is defined almost everywhere by the face normals (equivalently by the Lipschitz charts).

Fix a finite Lipschitz graph atlas $\{(U_j,\psi_j)\}_{j=1}^J$, with surface parametrizations $\Phi_j(z)=(z,\psi_j(z))$ in the rigid chart coordinates, and a subordinate finite Lipschitz partition of unity $\{\chi_j\}_{j=1}^J$ whose chartwise supports have positive distance from the chart edges. On $\mathbb R^2$, use the real subspace of the real-order Bessel-potential completion in [[def-real-order-bessel-potential-sobolev-space]]. Its published norm uses the weight $(1+|\xi|^2)^{1/2}$. Fix here the equivalent Hilbert norm
$$q(g)^2=\int_{\mathbb R^2}(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{1/2}|\widehat g(\xi)|^2d\xi.$$
The inequalities $(1+|\xi|^2)^{1/2}\le(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{1/2}\le2\pi(1+|\xi|^2)^{1/2}$ identify the same completion and classes under the negative-sign $2\pi$ Fourier convention of [[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-fractional-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]]. Define the real space $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ by requiring every localized chart pullback $g_j=(\chi_jg)\circ\Phi_j$, extended by zero outside its chart, to belong to that Euclidean space, and fix the **square-sum chart norm**
$$\|g\|_{H^{1/2}(\Gamma)}^2=\sum_{j=1}^J q(g_j)^2.$$
Its inner product is the sum of the real weighted Fourier inner products. This Hilbert norm is equivalent to the finite sum of chart norms: $(\sum_jq(g_j)^2)^{1/2}\le\sum_jq(g_j)\le\sqrt J(\sum_jq(g_j)^2)^{1/2}$. It controls $L^2(\Gamma)$, because graph surface Jacobians are bounded above and below and $g=\sum_j\chi_jg$. It is complete: a chart-norm Cauchy sequence has a global $L^2$ limit by that bound; its localized pullbacks converge in $L^2$ to the pullbacks of this limit, while completeness of each Euclidean weighted space gives convergence in each $q$ norm. The two limits agree, so the limit belongs to the defined chart space and convergence holds in the finite square sum.

Let real $H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$ be the continuous real dual, with its operator norm and pairing $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_\Gamma$; the dual of this real Hilbert space is Hilbert by [[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]. The interior and exterior traces of an $H^1$ function are denoted $\gamma^-u$ and $\gamma^+u$; their common chartwise trace space is $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ once the applicable trace theorem is proved. This chart-space definition applies to every compact Lipschitz surface in the stated geometry, including $C^2$ boundaries; a polyhedral trace theorem is used only in its stated polyhedral case.

The complex space is the Hilbert complexification of the real space: $\|g_1+ig_2\|^2=\|g_1\|^2+\|g_2\|^2$. Its $H^{-1/2}$ is the continuous conjugate dual, with pairing linear in the density and conjugate-linear in the trace, extending the real pairing. A complex density is a distribution via the **bilinear** test action $T_\lambda(v)=\langle\lambda,\overline v\rangle_\Gamma$. For either scalar field the continuous realization $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)\subset L^2(\Gamma)\subset H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$ uses $\langle f,g\rangle_\Gamma=\int_\Gamma f\overline g\,dS$ in the complex case and $\int_\Gamma fg\,dS$ in the real case. These inclusions follow from the just-proved $H^{1/2}\to L^2$ bound and Cauchy–Schwarz.

No smoothness at edges or vertices is included in this definition. The normal is only used almost everywhere, and on a polyhedral boundary every boundary integral is with respect to the sum of planar face-area measures; on a $C^2$ surface use the graph surface measure $\sqrt{1+|\nabla\psi_j|^2}\,dz$, with the chart partition.

## Definition

For $p\ge1$ and $g\in L^2(-1,1)$, define the degree-$(p-1)$ Legendre orthogonal projection
$$
\Pi_{p-1}g:=\sum_{n=0}^{p-1}\frac{2n+1}{2}\left(\int_{-1}^1g(t)P_n(t)\,dt\right)P_n.
$$
For $c\in\mathbb R$, define the endpoint-anchored integrated projector
$$
\mathcal I_p(c,g)(x):=c+\int_{-1}^x\Pi_{p-1}g(t)\,dt,\qquad -1\le x\le1.
$$
If an absolutely continuous function $f$ is represented as $f(x)=f(-1)+\int_{-1}^xf'(t)\,dt$ with $f'\in L^2$, write $I_pf:=\mathcal I_p(f(-1),f')$. The finite sum and integral are defined for every such input; no choice axiom is used in this definition.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f$ be finite convex, in the sense of [[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]], on an open convex $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$. At each $x\in U$ the subdifferential $\partial f(x)=\{p:f(y)\ge f(x)+p\cdot(y-x)\ (y\in U)\}$ is nonempty; it is locally bounded and its graph is locally closed. It is a singleton exactly when $f$ is differentiable, and then equals $\{Df(x)\}$. For every closed Euclidean ball $K\subset U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]) there is a finite globally Lipschitz convex $H$ ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]) on $\mathbb R^n$ equal to $f$ on $K$. For $F(x)=H(x)+|x|^2/2$, the conjugate $F^*(p)=\sup_x(p\cdot x-F(x))$ is finite and $C^1$, and $g=DF^*$ is globally one-Lipschitz with $g(p)=x$ iff $p\in\partial F(x)$.

1.1 At $x\in U$, the directional slope $d(v)=\lim_{t\downarrow0}[f(x+tv)-f(x)]/t$ exists and is finite: convexity makes these quotients monotone in $t$, while local Lipschitz continuity bounds them. Positive homogeneity follows by rescaling $t$. Convexity applied at the midpoint of $x+2tv$ and $x+2tw$ gives $d(v+w)\le d(v)+d(w)$. By [A1] and [F2], Hahn-Banach extends zero on $\{0\}$ to a linear functional $p\cdot v\le d(v)$. The chord inequality gives $d(y-x)\le f(y)-f(x)$, so $p\in\partial f(x)$. [A1, F1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 If $f$ is $L$-Lipschitz on a ball and $x$ lies in its concentric half ball, testing the support inequality at $x\pm te$ for every unit vector $e$ and sufficiently small $t>0$ gives $|p\cdot e|\le L$. Thus all its subgradients have norm at most $L$. On compact subsets this follows by a finite cover. If $x_j\to x$, $p_j\to p$, and $p_j\in\partial f(x_j)$, pass to the limit in every support inequality using continuity of $f$; hence $p\in\partial f(x)$. Differentiability gives $\partial f(x)=\{Df(x)\}$ by testing both signs of small increments. Conversely, if $\partial f(x)=\{p\}$, the local bound and [F3] imply that every choice $q_y\in\partial f(y)$ converges to $p$ as $y\to x$: otherwise [A1] selects a contrary sequence with a convergent subsequence whose limit is a different limiting subgradient. The inequalities $p\cdot h\le f(x+h)-f(x)\le q_{x+h}\cdot h$ then prove differentiability with derivative $p$. [A1, F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

## Statement

For tensors $A,B$ of the same finite shape, every mode unfolding and every cut unfolding preserves the Frobenius inner product and norm.

1.1 For a mode-$k$ unfolding, the map from a multi-index $(i_1,\ldots,i_d)$ to the matrix position consisting of row $i_k$ and the ordered tuple of all other indices is a bijection: the row and column tuple recover every original index exactly once. ## Statement

Let $P\subset\mathbb R^2$ be finite and nonempty, and define $V(p)=\{x:\|x-p\|^2\le\|x-q\|^2\ \text{for all }q\in P\}$. If $x$ belongs to at least three distinct cells, then all sites whose cells contain $x$ lie on one circle centered at $x$, no site lies strictly inside that circle, and their convex hull is a polygon with those sites as its vertices.

2.1 The common radius is positive, since radius zero would force every site whose cell contains $x$ to equal $x$, contradicting distinctness and the existence of three sites. A line intersects the circle $\|y-x\|^2=r^2$ in at most two points: parameterizing the line as $y=a+tv$ gives a nonzero quadratic equation in $t$. Hence no three of the sites on the circle are collinear. For any one such site $p$, the tangent line at $p$ supports the disk and meets the circle only at $p$; therefore $p$ cannot be a convex combination of the other circle sites. All nearest sites are extreme points of their convex hull, so that hull is a polygon with these sites as its vertices. [step 1.1, F1, algebra, algebra] ∎

## Statement

[[alg-sketch-and-solve-least-squares]]. In exact arithmetic, if its zero-
threshold SVD call converges and supplies an exact SVD record, the returned

## Statement

For every admissible input to
[[alg-strong-rrqr-interpolative-decomposition]], in either exact arithmetic or
its specified represented finite-precision mode, the procedure terminates
with exactly one listed algorithm status. The interior branch makes at most
$S$ swaps and at most $S+1$ score-test passes. In finite precision the reported
input rank is the exact rank of the represented matrix, not a numerical-rank
estimate for unrepresented data. Every certificate status is assigned in finite
work, without a search until success.

On a finite-precision successful interior branch, the direct certificate data
$(D,r^2,c^2)$ refer to the actual returned $J,T$ and satisfy

$$D=A-A(:,J)T,\qquad r^2=\sum_{a,b}|D_{ab}|^2,\qquad c^2=\max_{a,b}|T_{ab}|^2.$$

An ID-certificate status `certified` guarantees

$$T(:,J)=I_k,\qquad \max_{a,b}|T_{ab}|\le f,\qquad \|A-A(:,J)T\|_2\le\sqrt{r^2}.$$

This direct bound needs no successful RRQR certificate. It asserts no
singular-value-relative error bound for an uncertified RRQR candidate.

1.1 In the rank test [F1], each of the $n$ columns scans at most $m$ rows. A nonzero pivot is the only divisor used in a row elimination, so every exact rational operation is defined and has finite integer numerators and denominators. Row swaps and subtracting a multiple of one row from another are invertible operations; they preserve all linear dependence relations among columns. At completion the echelon matrix has $r$ nonzero rows with distinct pivot columns, and all remaining rows vanish. Its pivot columns are independent by triangular back-substitution, and its image is contained in the $r$-dimensional space of vectors supported on the nonzero rows. Its rank is therefore exactly $r$, which equals the original rank. The same finite argument applies to the represented selected-block singularity test. Thus no rounded pivot threshold or undecidable limiting test is involved in either finite-precision rank decision. In exact mode the same rank-preserving operations and finite pivot scans apply over the exact input field, using the assumed exact arithmetic and comparisons. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Each QR initialization or refactorization has finitely many pivot scans and at most $mn$ local updates by [F1]. Their scalar operations terminate individually in the specified model. A zero target is skipped, and division is performed only after its denominator check. An inadmissible rounded operation exits with `range-failure`; a singular selected block exits with `singular-selected-block`. Otherwise triangular solves and inverse-row calculations use finitely many nonzero diagonal divisions, and finitely many norms and comparisons produce a score-test pass. In exact arithmetic the corresponding finite QR eliminations, norms, and comparisons are defined by the exact model; the same singular-block branch prevents an undefined solve. [F1, given, step 1.1, algebra]

## Definition

Let $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $A\in F^{n\times n}$, $B\in F^{n\times m}$, $C\in F^{p\times n}$, and $R=R^*\in F^{m\times m}$ be positive definite. Write $Q=C^*C$ and $G=BR^{-1}B^*$. The inverse $R^{-1}$ is well-defined: [[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]] supplies an invertible factor $R=LL^*$, so $R^{-1}=L^{-*}L^{-1}$. Thus $v^*Gv=\|L^{-1}B^*v\|_2^2\ge0$ and $v^*Qv=\|Cv\|_2^2\ge0$. The symbol $^*$ is transpose over $\mathbb R$ and conjugate transpose over $\mathbb C$.

The **continuous algebraic Riccati equation (CARE)** is
$$A^*X+XA-XGX+Q=0.$$
Its residual is $F_c(X)=A^*X+XA-XGX+Q$, its feedback is $K_c(X)=R^{-1}B^*X$, and its closed-loop matrix is $A_c(X)=A-BK_c(X)=A-GX$.

For $X=X^*\succeq0$, $S_X:=R+B^*XB$ is positive definite because
$v^*S_Xv=v^*Rv+(Bv)^*X(Bv)>0$ for every nonzero $v$. The **discrete
algebraic Riccati equation (DARE)** is
$$X=Q+A^*XA-A^*XB(R+B^*XB)^{-1}B^*XA.$$
Its residual is $F_d(X)=Q+A^*XA-A^*XB(R+B^*XB)^{-1}B^*XA-X$. Whenever $X=X^*$, the matrix $R+B^*XB$ is positive definite if $X\succeq0$. Its feedback and closed-loop matrix are
$$K_d(X)=(R+B^*XB)^{-1}B^*XA,\qquad A_c(X)=A-BK_d(X).$$
A CARE solution is **stabilizing** when it is Hermitian and $A_c(X)$ is Hurwitz. A DARE solution is **stabilizing** when it is Hermitian, $R+B^*XB\succ0$, and $A_c(X)$ is Schur stable. No inverse of $A$ is part of either definition.

For Hermitian $X$ with $S_X$ invertible, multiplication gives
$$(I+GX)^{-1}=I-BS_X^{-1}B^*X,\qquad X(I+GX)^{-1}=X-XB S_X^{-1}B^*X.$$
In either product, the additional coefficient of $B$ is
$R^{-1}-S_X^{-1}-S_X^{-1}(B^*XB)R^{-1}=0$, because
$S_X=R+B^*XB$. Thus the DARE is equivalently
$X=Q+A^*X(I+GX)^{-1}A$, and its closed-loop matrix is
$A_c(X)=(I+GX)^{-1}A$.

The associated homogeneous symplectic pencil is
$$N=\begin{bmatrix}A&0\\-Q&I\end{bmatrix},\qquad M=\begin{bmatrix}I&G\\0&A^*\end{bmatrix},\qquad \mathcal P(\alpha,\beta)=\beta N-\alpha M.$$
The homogeneous-coordinate convention is that a finite eigenvalue
$\lambda$ is $[\alpha:\beta]=[\lambda:1]$ and $[1:0]$ denotes infinity.

## Statement

Let $G\in\mathbb R^{n\times q}$, with $q\ge n$, be an exact prediction or
measurement prearray. Let $\widehat G$ be its computed version and assume
$$\|\widehat G-G\|_F\le e_{\mathrm{form}}+e_{\mathrm{in}},$$
where $e_{\mathrm{form}},e_{\mathrm{in}}\ge0$, $e_{\mathrm{form}}$ bounds
rounded products used to form the array, and $e_{\mathrm{in}}$ bounds
separately specified input-factor uncertainty. If
the successful scaled-Householder QR of $\widehat G^T\in\mathbb R^{q\times
n}$ has reduced upper factor $R$ and $L=R^T$, set
$$\kappa_q=\kappa_q(u),\qquad \beta_{q,n}=(1+\kappa_q)^n-1,\qquad \epsilon=e_{\mathrm{form}}+e_{\mathrm{in}}+ \beta_{q,n}\|\widehat G\|_F,$$
where $\kappa_q$ is the explicit local coefficient in
[[lem-scaled-householder-step-meets-local-backward-error-premise]]. Then
$$\|LL^T-GG^T\|_F\le2\|G\|_F\epsilon+\epsilon^2.$$
If $200qnu<1$, the rational envelope lemma
[[lem-square-root-kalman-householder-error-rational-envelope]] gives
$\beta_{q,n}\le\eta_{q,n}:=200qnu/(1-200qnu)$. In that regime the same
conclusion holds with
$\epsilon=e_{\mathrm{form}}+e_{\mathrm{in}}+\eta_{q,n}\|\widehat G\|_F$.
For one left-to-right rounded product $\widehat{UV}$ with inner dimension
$r$ and $ru<1$, a valid choice is
$e_{\mathrm{form}}=\gamma_r\|U\|_F\|V\|_F$; for several disjoint product
blocks, sum these bounds. This conclusion allows rank loss and does not imply
that the nearby joint covariance has the original independent-noise block
structure.

2.1 Apply [F3] to the factor identity and perturbation $E$ from step 1.2. It gives $\|LL^T-GG^T\|_F\le2\|G\|_F\epsilon+\epsilon^2$ for the stated $\beta_{q,n}$ choice. Under $200qnu<1$, [F4] makes this epsilon no larger than the version using $\eta_{q,n}$. Since $t\mapsto2\|G\|_Ft+t^2$ is increasing for $t\ge0$, the same covariance bound follows with the rational-envelope epsilon. The argument permits zero singular values and places no structural restriction on the perturbation of $GG^T$. [F3, F4, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$, $d\in\{2,3\}$, be a connected polygonal or polyhedral domain with a finite conforming affine simplicial mesh $\mathcal T_h$ and no essential boundary constraints. Define the continuous P1 vector space $S_h=\{v\in C^0(\overline D;\mathbb R^d):v|_K\text{ is affine for every }K\in\mathcal T_h\}$ and its global nodal basis $(\phi_i)_{i=1}^N$. For constants $\mu>0$ and $\lambda\ge0$, set $\varepsilon(v)=(\nabla v+\nabla v^T)/2$, $k(v,w)=2\mu\int_D\varepsilon(v):\varepsilon(w)+\lambda\int_D\operatorname{div}v\,\operatorname{div}w$, and $K_{ij}=k(\phi_j,\phi_i)$. For every infinitesimal rigid motion $r(x)=a+\Omega x$, with $a\in\mathbb R^d$ and $\Omega^T=-\Omega$, its nodal coefficient vector lies in $\ker K$. Thus the range of any complete nullspace basis supplied to [[alg-linear-elasticity-rigid-body-nullspace-gauge]] must contain these translation and rotation vectors. This example does not claim they exhaust the nullspace on every mesh.

2.1 Since $\Omega$ is skew-symmetric, $\varepsilon(r)=(\Omega+\Omega^T)/2=0$ and $\operatorname{div}r=\operatorname{tr}\Omega=0$. Thus the stiffness bilinear form pairs $r$ to zero with every test basis function, which is exactly $Kr=0$ in coefficient coordinates. By [F1], every complete gauge basis must span these null vectors, although other null modes are not excluded here. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let
$(V,H,J)$ be a Banach evolution triple with compact inclusion
$i:V\Subset H$ and continuous canonical inclusion $J:H\hookrightarrow V^*$.
Let $T<\infty$, $1<p<\infty$, and $1<q\le\infty$. Suppose
$u_j\in L^p(0,T;V)$ have distributional derivatives
$u_j'\in L^q(0,T;V^*)$ and
$$\sup_j\bigl(\|u_j\|_{L^p(0,T;V)}+\|u_j'\|_{L^q(0,T;V^*)}\bigr)<\infty.$$
Then $(u_j)$ is relatively compact in $L^p(0,T;H)$. If also
$\sup_j\|u_j\|_{L^\infty(0,T;H)}<\infty$, each subsequence converging in
$L^p(0,T;H)$ converges, after the same subsequence, in every
$L^r(0,T;H)$ with $1\le r<\infty$.

1.1 Fix $\varepsilon>0$. Compactness in [F1] makes the image in $H$ of the $V$ unit ball totally bounded. Choose finitely many points from $i(V)$ within $\varepsilon$ of that image, and let $E\subset i(V)$ be their finite-dimensional span. If $P_E$ is the $H$-orthogonal projection, its best-approximation property gives $$\|(I-P_E)iv\|_H\le\varepsilon\|v\|_V\qquad(v\in V).$$ After orthonormalizing a basis, write $e_\ell=iv_\ell$ with $v_\ell\in V$. [A1, F1, given, choose]

2.1 The finitely many coefficient functions of $P_Eu_j$ are uniformly bounded and share the modulus from step 1.2. Choose a finite time grid so the modulus between adjacent grid points is below $\varepsilon$, and finite $\varepsilon$-nets for their bounded values at each grid point. Rounding those values gives a finite $\varepsilon$-net in the uniform norm for the coefficient vectors, hence $\{P_Eu_j\}$ is totally bounded in $L^p(0,T;H)$. [A1, F3, step 1.2, choose]

The auxiliary projection span can be the zero space when the embedded unit ball needs no nonzero approximation directions; its coefficient list is then empty and the remainder estimate still controls the family.

## Definition

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega$ be a bounded domain and let $1/2<s\le1$. Say that $\Omega$ has
a **Dirichlet Poisson smoothing index $s$** with constant $C_{\rm reg}$ if,
for every $g\in L^2(\Omega)$, there is a unique $\zeta_g\in H^1_0(\Omega)$
satisfying
$$\int_\Omega\nabla\zeta_g\cdot\nabla v\,dx =\int_\Omega g v\,dx\qquad(v\in H^1_0(\Omega)),$$
and $\zeta_g\in H^{1+s}(\Omega)$ with
$$\|\zeta_g\|_{H^{1+s}(\Omega)}\le C_{\rm reg}\|g\|_{L^2(\Omega)}.$$
This is a hypothesis about the continuous adjoint Poisson problem. It is not
asserted for every bounded domain.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and that $\Gamma$ is polyhedral as specified in [[def-bem-lipschitz-polyhedral-boundary-and-trace-spaces]]. The interior trace $\gamma^-:H^1(\Omega^-)\to H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ is bounded. On every bounded exterior boundary collar $C=\Omega^+\cap U$, where $U$ is a bounded neighborhood of $\Gamma$ with Lipschitz collar boundary, the exterior trace $\gamma^+:H^1(C)\to H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ is bounded. The corresponding localized assertion holds over each boundary chart. Thus an exterior function has this trace whenever it is $H^1$ up to the boundary on such collars; membership in $H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega^+)$ alone does not assert a boundary trace. There is a bounded linear right inverse $L:H^{1/2}(\Gamma)\to H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ with $\gamma(Lg)=g$. There is also a bounded extension operator $E:H^1(\Omega^-)\to H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ with $(Eu)|_{\Omega^-}=u$.

Let $\dot H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ denote the completion of $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ in the norm $\|u\|_{\dot H^1}=\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}$. Its elements have an $L^6$ representative, the trace $\gamma:\dot H^1(\mathbb R^3)\to H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ is bounded, and the right inverse above may be chosen with compact support near $\Gamma$.

3.1 Flattening a polyhedral chart. Refine a chart into its finitely many planar sectors so that $\psi$ is affine on each sector. There $\Phi(x',t)=(x',t+\psi(x'))$ is affine with determinant $1$, and its inverse is affine. By [F6] volume substitution and [F7] the chain rule, composition changes the $H^1$ norm by at most a chart-dependent factor. On each planar boundary sector, the surface Jacobian is constant and distances in graph coordinates and physical coordinates are comparable because $\Phi$ and its inverse are Lipschitz. Substitution in the double integral defining $H^{1/2}$ therefore compares the Slobodeckij chart seminorms in both directions; [F8] transfers this comparison to the fixed Bessel chart norm. The finite partition in the definition fixes chart overlaps. Applying steps 1.1 and 2.1 to every localized chart piece and summing proves the trace bounds and constructs a bounded right inverse; compact chart cutoffs keep each lift in its chart. For every localized flat half-box the $H^1$-convergent smooth approximants in [F92] extend the flat estimates by continuity. For the physical polyhedral chart pieces, apply [F92] there first; piecewise affine substitution and the displayed derivative bound pass the approximants to the flattened chart in $H^1$. Across a shared planar sector, the two restrictions have the common value of the composed ambient smooth function; integrating by parts cancels their interface terms, so the piecewise chain-rule gradient is the global weak gradient. The uniform bounds extend this identity to the $H^1$ limit. This supplies the approximation and weak-coordinate argument at edges as well as on face interiors. [F6, F7, F8, F92, step 1.1, step 2.1, given, algebra]

4.1 Extension from the bounded domain. On each flattened chart, reflect an $H^1$ function evenly across $t=0$. For smooth functions the affine changes and chain rule [F6, F7] bound the reflected $H^1$ norm by the original norm; flat reflection preserves the integral of $|u|^2+|\nabla u|^2$ up to factor $2$. Approximation on the flat half-space from step 3.1 extends this bound to all $H^1$ functions. A finite partition of unity combines these local reflections with the unchanged interior function and a cutoff outside a fixed bounded neighborhood, giving a bounded operator $E:H^1(\Omega^-)\to H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ equal to $u$ on $\Omega^-$. The same local chart construction on bounded exterior collars proves the stated exterior trace bound. In a flattened collar, the one-dimensional fundamental theorem and Cauchy–Schwarz give $\|f(\cdot,t)-\gamma f\|_{L^2(K)}^2\le t\int_0^t\|\partial_s f(\cdot,s)\|_{L^2(K)}^2ds$ for a compact tangential set $K$ and $t>0$, with $f(\cdot,t)$ parametrized by nonnegative normal distance into the chosen side; approximation passes this to $H^1$ functions. Consequently the trace of a continuous $H^1$ representative is its pointwise boundary restriction, since continuity gives the same local $L^2$ limit. [F6, F7, step 3.1, given, construct]

Assume Countable Choice. Under the finite partition hypotheses of [[def-intersection-volume-conservative-remapping]], let $P_0(\mathcal T)$ be the target cellwise-constant subspace of $L^2(\Omega)$. For every source piecewise-constant $v$, $Rv$ is the $L^2$ orthogonal projection of $v$ onto $P_0(\mathcal T)$, hence $\|Rv\|_2\le\|v\|_2$. It preserves total mass, $\int_\Omega Rv=\int_\Omega v$, and if all $v_i\ge0$ then every target value $(Rv)_j\ge0$.

1.1 By [F4], Lebesgue measure is countably additive and hence finitely additive. The partition hypotheses therefore give $\sum_iw_{ji}=|T_j|$ for every target cell and $\sum_jw_{ji}=|S_i|$ for every source cell; omitted partition boundaries are null and do not change these measures. The same finite additivity gives $\int_{T_j}v=\sum_iw_{ji}v_i$. [F1, F4, A1, given]

3.1 Orthogonality with $z=Rv$ gives $\|v\|_2^2=\|Rv\|_2^2+\|v-Rv\|_2^2$, so $\|Rv\|_2\le\|v\|_2$. All terms are finite because the partitions are finite, cells have finite volume, and $v$ is piecewise constant. [F2, step 2.1, algebra]

## Statement

Let $J\ge3$, $N=2^J$, $s>0$, and $p=(s+1/2)^{-1}\in(0,2)$. Let $U\in\mathbb R^{N\times N}$ be orthogonal, $x\in\mathbb R^N$, and $c=Ux$. Regard $c$ as one coarse block $a\in\mathbb R^4$ and detail blocks $d_j\in\mathbb R^{2^j}$ for $2\le j\le J-1$, with the norm of [[def-na-wavelet-coefficient-besov-quasinorm]]. For $1\le m\le N$, hard retention of the $m$ largest coefficients has reconstruction error
$$\|x-U^TH_m(c)\|_2\le \sqrt{\frac{p}{2-p}}\,\|c\|_{b^s_{p,p}(J)}\,m^{-s},$$
where $c=Ux$ and $U$ is the orthogonal analysis matrix.

2.1 By [F2], the squared best m-term error is $\sum_{n=m+1}^N b_n^2$. Because $2/p>1$, the decreasing function $t^{-2/p}$ satisfies $\sum_{n=m+1}^N n^{-2/p}\le\int_m^\infty t^{-2/p}\,dt=\frac{p}{2-p}m^{1-2/p}.$ Combining this with step 1.1 and taking square roots gives a factor $m^{1/2-1/p}=m^{-s}$, since $1/p=s+1/2$. When $m=N$, the actual error is zero by retaining every coefficient, so the bound still holds. [given, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For each $N\ge3$, let $C_N=C(c)$ be the periodic cycle Laplacian circulant generated by $c_0=2$, $c_1=-1$, $c_{N-1}=-1$, and $c_j=0$ otherwise. With $\omega=e^{-2\pi i/N}$, its Fourier eigenvalues are $\lambda_k=2-\omega^k-\omega^{-k}$. Exactly $\lambda_0$ vanishes, so $C_Nx=f$ is solvable exactly when $\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}f_j=0$; on the zero-mean subspace the solution is unique. For $N=4$ and $f=(1,-1,1,-1)^T$, the solution is $x=f/4$.

2.1 Put $z=\omega^k$. It is nonzero by [F3], and $$\lambda_k=0\iff z+z^{-1}=2\iff (z-1)^2=0\iff z=1,$$ where the middle equivalence follows after multiplying by $z$, and the last uses [F4]. By the exponential kernel characterization in [F3], $\omega^k=1$ exactly when $-2\pi i k/N\in2\pi i\mathbb Z$, equivalently $k/N$ is an integer. For $0\le k<N$ this means $k=0$. Thus only the constant Fourier mode is a zero mode. [given, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 At $k=0$, $(\mathcal F_N f)_0=N^{-1/2}\sum_j f_j$. Hence [F2] gives solvability precisely when $\sum_j f_j=0$. All nonzero modes then determine $\mathcal F_Nx$ uniquely, while the zero-mode coordinate is free; imposing $\sum_jx_j=0$ fixes that coordinate to zero, proving uniqueness on the zero-mean subspace. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

## Statement refuted

Every finite tensor has a best Frobenius approximation among tensors of CP rank at most two.

2.1 Suppose $W$ had a two-term expression $a\otimes b\otimes c+a'\otimes b'\otimes c'$. The first-mode slices being independent forces $a,a'$ to be independent. If $b,b'$ or $c,c'$ were dependent, every linear combination of the two slices would have matrix rank at most one, so its determinant would vanish identically, contrary to $\det(xW_1+yW_2)=-x^2$. Thus both pairs are independent. For any $x,y$, the pencil slice is $(xa_1+ya_2)bc^{\mathsf T}+(xa'_1+ya'_2)b'c'^{\mathsf T}$. Its determinant is a nonzero constant times $(xa_1+ya_2)(xa'_1+ya'_2)$. Independence of $a,a'$ makes the two linear factors nonproportional, so this determinant has two distinct zero lines; it cannot equal $-x^2$, which vanishes on the repeated line $x=0$. This contradiction proves $\operatorname{rank}_{CP}(W)>2$, hence it is exactly three. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For every $\varepsilon>0$, define $W_\varepsilon=\varepsilon^{-1}\bigl((e_1+\varepsilon e_2)^{\otimes3}-e_1^{\otimes3}\bigr)$. This is a difference of two elementary tensors, with the scalar absorbed into one factor, so its CP rank is at most two. Expanding gives $W_\varepsilon=W+\varepsilon(e_2\otimes e_2\otimes e_1+e_2\otimes e_1\otimes e_2+e_1\otimes e_2\otimes e_2)+\varepsilon^2e_2^{\otimes3}$, so $\|W_\varepsilon-W\|_F\to0$. Thus the infimal rank-two approximation error is zero. Since step 2.1 shows $W$ itself has rank three, no rank-at-most-two tensor attains that infimum. [F1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $A\in F^{m\times n}$, $k\ge1$, and $k<\ell\le\min(m,n)$. Partition an
$n\times\ell$ matrix $\Omega$ in right-singular-vector coordinates as
$V^*\Omega=[\Omega_1^T\ \Omega_2^T]^T$, where $\Omega_1\in F^{k\times\ell}$
has full row rank. If $Q$ is any orthonormal basis of $\operatorname{Ran}(A\Omega)$,
then
$$\|(I-QQ^*)A\|_2\le\sigma_{k+1}+\|\Sigma_2\Omega_2\Omega_1^\dagger\|_2,$$
where $A=U\Sigma V^*$ is an SVD, $\Sigma_2$ is the trailing block, and
$\sigma_{k+1}=0$ when fewer than $k+1$ singular values are positive. No
inverse of the leading singular-value block is used, so this includes
$\operatorname{rank}(A)<k$.

2.1 Since $\Omega_1$ has full row rank, put $\Omega_1^\dagger=\Omega_1^*(\Omega_1\Omega_1^*)^{-1}$, so $\Omega_1\Omega_1^\dagger=I_k$. Let $Y=\Sigma[\Omega_1^T\ \Omega_2^T]^T$ and $C=Y\Omega_1^\dagger[I_k\ 0]$. The range of $C$ lies in $\operatorname{Ran}(Y)$, hence $(I-P)C=0$. [step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 The first $k$ rows of $\Sigma-C$ vanish because $\Omega_1\Omega_1^\dagger=I_k$, and the remaining rows form $[-\Sigma_2\Omega_2\Omega_1^\dagger\ \ \Sigma_2]$. Thus $\|(I-P)\Sigma\|_2=\|(I-P)(\Sigma-C)\|_2\le\|\Sigma-C\|_2\le\|\Sigma_2\Omega_2\Omega_1^\dagger\|_2+\|\Sigma_2\|_2$: the horizontal block is a sum of two zero-padded blocks, so the triangle inequality applies. By [F1] and [F4], $\|\Sigma_2\|_2=\sigma_{k+1}$, including zero-tail and rank-deficient cases. [step 2.1, F1, F3, F4, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For real endpoints $a<b$, $\omega\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, and an integer $m\ge0$, the output of [[alg-na-fourier-polynomial-moments]] satisfies $\mu_k=\int_a^b x^k e^{i\omega x}\,dx$ for every $0\le k\le m$, with
$$\mu_0=\frac{e^{i\omega b}-e^{i\omega a}}{i\omega},\qquad \mu_k=\frac{b^ke^{i\omega b}-a^ke^{i\omega a}}{i\omega}-\frac{k}{i\omega}\mu_{k-1}\quad(k\ge1).$$
Thus all polynomial moments for the Fourier phase $g(x)=x$ are obtained by a finite exact recurrence.

1.1 The algorithm sets $\mu_0=(e^{i\omega b}-e^{i\omega a})/(i\omega)$. Since $(e^{i\omega x}/(i\omega))'=e^{i\omega x}$ by [F2], [F3] with $u=1$ identifies this value with $\int_a^b e^{i\omega x}\,dx$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

## Statement

For real endpoints $a<b$, $\omega\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, and an integer $m\ge0$, the output of [[alg-na-fourier-polynomial-moments]] satisfies $\mu_k=\int_a^b x^k e^{i\omega x}\,dx$ for every $0\le k\le m$, with
$$\mu_0=\frac{e^{i\omega b}-e^{i\omega a}}{i\omega},\qquad \mu_k=\frac{b^ke^{i\omega b}-a^ke^{i\omega a}}{i\omega}-\frac{k}{i\omega}\mu_{k-1}\quad(k\ge1).$$
Thus all polynomial moments for the Fourier phase $g(x)=x$ are obtained by a finite exact recurrence.

1.1 The algorithm sets $\mu_0=(e^{i\omega b}-e^{i\omega a})/(i\omega)$. Since $(e^{i\omega x}/(i\omega))'=e^{i\omega x}$ by [F2], [F3] with $u=1$ identifies this value with $\int_a^b e^{i\omega x}\,dx$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice for the finite-dimensional Gaussian probability law.
Let $1\le d\le n$, $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$U\subseteq\mathbb K^n$ be a fixed $d$-dimensional subspace. Let
$G\in\mathbb K^{m\times n}$ have iid standard real Gaussian entries when
$\mathbb K=\mathbb R$, or iid normalized complex Gaussian entries with
$\mathbb E|g|^2=1$ when $\mathbb K=\mathbb C$. Put $S=G/\sqrt m$.
For $0<\varepsilon,\delta<1$, if
$$
m\ge192\varepsilon^{-2}\bigl(d+\log(1/\delta)\bigr),
$$
then with probability at least $1-\delta$, $S$ is an
$\varepsilon$-subspace embedding for $U$. Thus this Gaussian distribution
is an $(\varepsilon,\delta)$ oblivious $\ell_2$ subspace embedding for
dimension $d$.

3.1 On the complementary event, put $H=Q^*S^*SQ-I_d$. This is Hermitian and $|v^*Hv|=|\|SQv\|_2^2-1|<\varepsilon/2$ for every $v\in\mathcal N$. By [F6], $\|H\|_2\le\varepsilon$. For nonzero $y$, [F7] and [F8] give $|y^*Hy|\le\|y\|_2\|Hy\|_2\le\|H\|_2\|y\|_2^2$; the zero vector satisfies the same inequality. Therefore $(1-\varepsilon)\|y\|_2^2\le\|SQy\|_2^2\le(1+\varepsilon)\|y\|_2^2$. Since $Q$ is an isometry onto $U$, [F1] identifies this as the required embedding inequality for every $x=Qy\in U$. [F1, F6, F7, F8, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$, $s\ge0$, $A\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$ be Hermitian positive semidefinite, and $S\in\mathbb F^{n\times s}$. In the Loewner order, where $B\preceq C$ means $C-B$ is positive semidefinite, the Nyström approximation in [[def-psd-nystrom-approximation]] satisfies
$0\preceq\widehat A_{\mathrm{nys}}\preceq A$.
If the selected columns capture the range in the sense that $\operatorname{Ran}(AS)=\operatorname{Ran}(A)$, then $\widehat A_{\mathrm{nys}}=A$. Here rank, when used in the proof, means dimension of the range.

1.1 Put $M=A^{1/2}$ and $P=P_{\operatorname{Ran}(MS)}$. By [F1], for every vector $x$, $x^*\widehat A_{\mathrm{nys}}x=\|PMx\|_2^2\ge0$ and $x^*(A-\widehat A_{\mathrm{nys}})x=\|(I-P)Mx\|_2^2\ge0$. Both matrices are Hermitian, so these quadratic-form inequalities prove $0\preceq\widehat A_{\mathrm{nys}}\preceq A$. [F1, F3, algebra]

## Statement

Let $(U_j^{m,n})$ be a scheme from
[[def-conservative-finite-volume-scheme]], with reconstruction
$(\mathcal U_m,\mathcal Q_m)$ as in
[[def-finite-volume-space-time-reconstruction]]. For a test function
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R\times(-\infty,T))$, define its space-time
cell average
$$ \Phi_j^{m,n}=\frac1{h_m\tau_m}\int_{t_n^m}^{t_{n+1}^m}\int_{I_j^m}\varphi(x,t)\,dx\,dt. $$ If $N\ge1$ is such that $\varphi$ vanishes for $t\ge t_{N-1}^m$, then $$ \sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}h_m U_j^{m,0}\Phi_j^{m,0} +\sum_{n=1}^{N-1}\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}h_m U_j^{m,n} (\Phi_j^{m,n}-\Phi_j^{m,n-1}) +\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}\tau_m Q_{j+1/2}^{m,n} (\Phi_{j+1}^{m,n}-\Phi_j^{m,n})=0. $$
All sums are finite because $\varphi$ is compactly supported in space and time.
1.1 Multiply [F1] by $\Phi_j^{m,n}$ and sum over $j\in\mathbb Z$ and $n=0,\ldots,N-1$. Only finitely many terms are nonzero, so the summed update is an exact finite sum equal to zero. [F1, F2, given]

3.1 Reindex the spatial flux sum: $$ \sum_j(Q_{j+1/2}^{m,n}-Q_{j-1/2}^{m,n})\Phi_j^{m,n} =\sum_jQ_{j+1/2}^{m,n}(\Phi_j^{m,n}-\Phi_{j+1}^{m,n}). $$ Substitute this and step 2.1 into step 1.1, then multiply the zero identity by $-1$ to obtain exactly the displayed formula. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎
cases.evidence: Finite support permits exact temporal telescoping and spatial reindexing of conservative updates into the discrete weak identity. At the smallest horizon the interior time-difference sum is empty, and zero test support can also make every spatial contribution vanish.

Each row therefore equals the matching component of $(u\pm c)r_\pm$, using $H=u^2/2+c^2/(\gamma-1)$. Since $c>0$, the eigenvalues are distinct and strictly ordered. [step 1.1, algebra]

Therefore the stated directional derivatives of $u-c,u,u+c$ follow. [step 1.1, F1, F2, algebra]

## Definition

Let $K$ be a cell in the one-dimensional interval or $d\ge2$ matching affine-simplex branch of [[def-pe04-upwind-dg-transport-discretization]], and fix an integer degree $p\ge0$. Let $(K,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a finite measure space as in [[def-measure-space]], let $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ have the raw measurable-function meaning of [[def-calligraphic-l-p-on-a-measure-space]], and let $W=\mathbb P_p(K)\subseteq\mathcal L^2(\mu)$. For $u\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ define its **cellwise L2 projection relation** to be the set
$$\mathcal P_K(u)=\left\{p\in\mathbb P_p(K):\int_K(u-p)w\,d\mu=0\text{ for every }w\in\mathbb P_p(K)\right\}.$$
For a mesh, the broken relation is the product of these cell relations. The measure $\mu$ is required to give positive measure to every nonempty relatively open subset of $K$ when existence and uniqueness are claimed. This definition does not itself assert that the set is a singleton. Whenever a later result proves that the relation has a unique member, write $\Pi_Ku$ for that member.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded connected contractible Lipschitz polyhedron. If $u\in H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ has distributional curl zero, then there is $p\in H^1(\Omega)$ with $u=\nabla p$ almost everywhere; $p$ is unique up to an additive constant.

1.1 By [F1] choose $f\in H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ with $\nabla f=u$. It remains to prove global integrability; local weak exactness alone is insufficient. Fix a ball $B\Subset\Omega$. For $M>0$ let $f_M=\max(-M,\min(f,M))$. By [F3] locally, $f_M\in H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$, $|\nabla f_M|\le|u|$, and $|f_M|\le M$. Since $\Omega$ has finite measure, these local derivative identities give global $H^1(\Omega)$ membership: the function is globally $L^2$, its locally specified derivatives are globally $L^2$, and every compactly supported test uses only finitely many local identities. Thus [F2] gives $\|f_M-(f_M)_\Omega\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C_\Omega\|u\|_2$. [F1, F2, F3, construct]

2.1 Put $a_M=(f_M)_\Omega$ and $b_M=(f_M)_B$. The preceding estimate gives $|a_M-b_M|\le |B|^{-1/2}C_\Omega\|u\|_2$. Therefore $\|f_M-b_M\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C_\Omega(1+|\Omega|^{1/2}|B|^{-1/2})\|u\|_2.$ On $B$, $f\in L^2$ and $|f_M|\le|f|$, so dominated convergence gives $b_M\to f_B$. Along the integers $M\to\infty$, $f_M\to f$ almost everywhere; Fatou's lemma applied to the displayed bound yields $f-f_B\in L^2(\Omega)$. Its weak gradient is $u\in L^2$, hence $p=f-f_B\in H^1(\Omega)$. If two such $p$ exist, their difference has zero weak gradient, and [F3] makes it constant on connected $\Omega$. This proves every original analytic and geometric clause. [F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Use the weighted network data of
[[def-finite-weighted-network-diffusion-data]]. The exact-arithmetic
conjugate-gradient result
[[thm-conjugate-gradient-is-the-krylov-galerkin-method-and-minimizes-the-energy-error]]
applies to each of the following systems:

1. $M+\tau L_D$ for every $\tau>0$;
2. the grounded steady matrix $L_D$ if every positive-conductance component
   containing a free vertex also meets the Dirichlet set $D$;
3. the closed Neumann matrix $L_C$ restricted to $K^\perp$, where
   $K=\ker L_C$, for every compatible right-hand side $b\in K^\perp$.

In case 3 the gauge $u\in K^\perp$ gives the unique solution of $L_Cu=b$.
Here $K^\perp$ uses the standard Euclidean inner product
$\langle x,y\rangle=x^{\mathsf T}y$. If a stated unknown space is
zero-dimensional, its solver claim is vacuous.
These are exact-arithmetic applicability claims only; no finite-precision
stability claim is made.

1.2 In the closed case, let $K=\ker L_C$. Symmetry implies $L_C(K^\perp)\subseteq K^\perp$: for $x\in K^\perp$ and $k\in K$, $k^{\mathsf T}L_Cx=(L_Ck)^{\mathsf T}x=0$. If a vector $x\in K^\perp$ has $x^{\mathsf T}L_Cx=0$, [F1] puts $x$ in $K$; hence $x=0$. Therefore the restriction $L_C|_{K^\perp}$ is positive definite. It has trivial kernel and is an endomorphism of the finite-dimensional space $K^\perp$, so [F2] makes it onto. Thus each $b\in K^\perp$ has one gauged solution $u\in K^\perp$. By [F5], an orthonormal basis of $K^\perp$ identifies this restriction with a real symmetric positive definite matrix, including the zero-dimensional case. [F1, F2, F5, given, algebra]

## Statement

For a level-$j$ invocation of [[alg-fas-vw-cycle]], let $u^*$ satisfy
$F_j(u^*)=f_j$. Suppose each selected pre/post smoother leaves every exact
root fixed, every restriction $I_ju^*$ lies in $U_{j-1}$ and is selected as
the exact coarse root at its zero-defect target, and the base solver returns
any initial exact root unchanged. Then the exact-branch FAS V/W cycle leaves
$u^*$ fixed. This holds for arbitrary admissible transfer maps $I_j,R_j,P_j$;
no identity such as $R_j=I_j$ or $I_jP_j=I$ is needed.

1.1 At level $0$, the input is the exact root $u_0^*$ and the base solver sees zero residual. Its stated contract in [F1] returns that initial root unchanged. Thus the level-$0$ call fixes its exact root. [given, F1, base]

1.2 At a noncoarsest level, each pre-smoothing sweep leaves $u^*$ unchanged. Thus $f_j-F_j(u^*)=0$ and the restricted coarse target is $g_H=F_{j-1}(I_j u^*)$. The hypothesis gives $I_j u^*\in U_{j-1}$ and selects it as the exact coarse root. The coarse call starts there, so [A1] makes each of the $\gamma_j$ recursive calls return $I_j u^*$; hence the prolongated difference is zero and every post-smoothing sweep fixes $u^*$. [given, F1, A1, ih, algebra]

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. For the connected exterior domain $\Omega^+$ of [[def-bem-lipschitz-polyhedral-boundary-and-trace-spaces]], let
$$E^+(\Omega^+)=\{u\in H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega^+):u\in L^6(\Omega^+),\ \nabla u\in L^2(\Omega^+)\}.$$
There is a constant $C$ depending only on $\Omega^-$ and its fixed trace atlas such that every $u\in E^+(\Omega^+)$ has $\gamma^+u\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ and
$$\|\gamma^+u\|_{H^{1/2}(\Gamma)}\le C\|\nabla u\|_{L^2(\Omega^+)}.$$

1.1 We justify the Sobolev slices. On each bounded spherical shell $a<|x|<b$ with $R/2<a<R<b$, $u$ belongs to $H^1$: bounded volume and $L^6$ give $L^2$, and its weak gradient is already $L^2$. Use [F4] to approximate it by ambient smooth $u_m$ in $H^1$ on a slightly larger shell. The polar formula [F90] and $a^2\le r^2\le b^2$ bound $\int_{S^2}\|u_m(r\omega)-u_l(r\omega)\|_{H^1(a,b)}^2d\sigma(\omega)$ by $C\|u_m-u_l\|_{H^1}^2$, because the radial derivative of a smooth approximant is $\omega\cdot\nabla u_m$. Take a subsequence with summable successive $H^1$ errors; Cauchy–Schwarz on the finite angular measure and Tonelli show that the successive slice norms are summable for almost every $\omega$. Completeness [F5] gives an $H^1(a,b)$ slice limit, identified by the polar $L^2$ limit with $u(r\omega)$ and derivative $\omega\cdot\nabla u(r\omega)$. Countably many overlapping shells exhaust $r>R/2$, so their representatives agree on overlaps off one angular null set; their values at $R$ define the usual trace, since the one-dimensional $H^1$ endpoint estimate passes smooth approximants to that value. By [F5] the slices are locally absolutely continuous. [A1, F3, F4, F5, F90, given, construct]

2.1 For almost every direction $\omega\in S^2$, the radial slice $r\mapsto u(r\omega)$ is locally H1 for $r\ge R$, and $\int_R^\infty|u(r\omega)|^6r^2dr<\infty$. Thus there is a sequence $r_m\to\infty$ with $u(r_m\omega)\to0$. For each such direction the radial derivative is square integrable with weight $r^2$; the one-dimensional fundamental theorem on $[R,r_m]$ and Cauchy–Schwarz give $|u(R\omega)|^2\le\left(\int_R^\infty|\partial_ru(r\omega)|^2r^2dr\right)\left(\int_R^\infty r^{-2}dr\right)=R^{-1}\int_R^\infty|\partial_ru(r\omega)|^2r^2dr.$ Integrating over $S^2$ by [F3,F90] yields $\|u\|_{L^2(\partial B_R)}\le R^{1/2}\|\nabla u\|_{L^2(\Omega^+\setminus B_R)}$. [A1, F3, F5, F90, step 1.1, given, choose]

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\widehat\Omega=[-1,1]^2$, let $\mathcal T_h$ be a matching shape-regular affine triangulation, and put $\Phi(x,y)=(x,y+x^2/4)$. Let $I_h$ be the vertexwise P1 interpolant and $\Phi_h(x,y)=(x,y+I_h(x^2/4))$. In the notation of [[def-curved-domain-geometry-approximation]], there is a constant $C$ depending only on the shape-regularity bound such that $e_0\le Ch^2$ and $e_1\le Ch$. For sufficiently small $h$, $\det D\Phi_h\ge1/2$, and $\Phi_h$ is globally one-to-one on the square. The exact map has $\det D\Phi=1$ and a global inverse $(X,Y)\mapsto(X,Y-X^2/4)$.

3.1 The first coordinate of $\Phi_h$ is $x$, and on each vertical segment its second coordinate is the continuous piecewise-affine function $y+I_h(x^2/4)(x,y)$. Its slope on every subsegment is $1+\partial_y I_h(x^2/4)\ge1-Ch$. Choose $h$ with $Ch\le1/2$. Integration over the finitely many subsegments makes this coordinate strictly increasing with increment at least half the vertical increment. Equal images must therefore have equal first coordinates and then equal second-coordinate inputs; hence $\Phi_h$ is injective. The same derivative estimate gives $\det D\Phi_h=1+\partial_yI_h(x^2/4)\ge1/2$. [F1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Fix an integer $N\ge4$, the unit torus, and $h=1/N$. Let $b=1$ and use final time $T=h$, but split it into $K$ steps of length $\Delta t=h/K$. The smooth periodic initial function
$$u_0(x):=\prod_{j=1}^{N-1}\frac{\sin^2(\pi(x-j/N))}{\sin^2(-\pi j/N)}$$
has grid samples $U_0^0=1$ and $U_j^0=0$ for $1\le j<N$. Exact transport over $T=h$ shifts those samples by exactly one node. The semi-Lagrangian method, however, performs $K$ fractional linear interpolations on the same fixed spatial grid.

1.1 Each denominator in $u_0$ is nonzero because $j/N\notin\mathbb Z$, each factor is smooth and $1$-periodic, and at node $x_0=0$ every factor equals $1$. At node $x_m=m/N$ with $1\le m<N$, the factor with $j=m$ vanishes. Thus the grid samples are exactly the stated unit vector. The exact characteristic is $X(t;s,x)=x+(t-s)$, so at $T=h$ the exact grid vector has value $1$ at node $1$ and $0$ at node $2$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Since $\binom K2K^{-2}\to1/2$ and $(1-1/K)^{K-2}=(1-1/K)^K/(1-1/K)^2\to e^{-1}$ by [F2], we have $\liminf_{K\to\infty}U_2^K\ge e^{-1}/2>0$, whereas the exact value at node $2$ is zero. Thus reducing $\Delta t$ at fixed $h$ does not remove this interpolation error. The sufficient condition $h^2/\Delta t\to0$ in the global error theorem cannot be dropped from that bound: here $h^2/\Delta t=hK\to\infty$. [given, F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $b\in C^1([0,T]\times\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^d)$ be periodic in space, and set
$$M:=\sup\|b\|_2,\qquad L_x:=\sup\|D_xb\|,\qquad L_t:=\sup\|\partial_tb\|_2,$$
where the suprema are over one full periodic time-space cylinder. For $0\le t_n<t_{n+1}\le T$, $\Delta t=t_{n+1}-t_n$, and an arrival lift $x$, let $X(t_n;t_{n+1},x)$ be the exact backward characteristic foot. The explicit Euler foot $x-\Delta t\,b(t_{n+1},x)$ satisfies
$$\bigl\|X(t_n;t_{n+1},x)-(x-\Delta t\,b(t_{n+1},x))\bigr\|_2\le\frac12(L_xM+L_t)(\Delta t)^2.$$
The estimate is local for every positive $\Delta t$; it requires no relation between displacement and grid width.

1.1 By [F2] and [F3], for $s\in[t_n,t_{n+1}]$ the backward characteristic satisfies $X(s)=x-\int_s^{t_{n+1}}b(X(r),r)\,dr$. Applying [F4] and the velocity bound gives $\|X(s)-x\|_2\le M(t_{n+1}-s)$. [given, F2, F3, F4]

## Statement

Let $I=[a,b]$ with $a<b$, let $m,n\ge0$, and let $f,w\in C(I,\mathbb R)$
with $w>0$ on $I$. A best rational approximant in
$\mathcal R_{m,n}^+(I)$ exists and is unique. For a candidate $r=p/q$ with
positive weighted error $E_r:=\|w(f-r)\|_{\infty,I}>0$, let
$N=N_{m,n}(r)=m+n-d_{m,n}(r)$. Then $r$ is best if and only if there are
$N+2$ ordered nodes $x_0<\cdots<x_{N+1}$ in $I$ and
$\sigma\in\{-1,1\}$ such that
$$w(x_i)(f(x_i)-r(x_i))=\sigma(-1)^iE_r\qquad(0\le i\le N+1).$$
If the best error is $0$, positivity of $w$ forces the unique best function
to be $f$ itself. In the normal case $d=0$ the count is $m+n+2$; for
defective candidates the count is $m+n+2-d$.

1.1 First suppose $E_r>0$ and that $r$ has $N+2$ alternating weighted extrema. If another admissible $s=p'/q'$ had strictly smaller weighted error, write $e_i=w(x_i)(f(x_i)-r(x_i))=\sigma(-1)^iE_r$ and $e_i'=w(x_i)(f(x_i)-s(x_i))$, so $|e_i'|<E_r$. Then $\sigma(-1)^i w(x_i)(s(x_i)-r(x_i))=E_r-\sigma(-1)^ie_i'>0$. Since $w(x_i)q(x_i)q'(x_i)>0$, the numerator $p'q-pq'$ has nonzero alternating signs at those nodes. It lies in $\mathcal P_N$ by [F3], contradicting [F6]. Thus no rational candidate has smaller weighted error and $r$ is best. [F1, F3, F6, given, algebra]

1.2 Now suppose $r$ is best with $E:=E_r>0$, and put $e=w(f-r)$. It is continuous by [F8], and [F10] makes $|e|$ attain $E$ on compact $I$, so its active-extrema set is nonempty and compact. If it had no $N+2$ alternating points, [F4] would give a polynomial $g\in\mathcal P_N$ with $e(x)g(x)>0$ on that set. By [F3], choose $u,v$ with $\deg u\le m$, $\deg v\le n$, and $g=uq-pv$. [F1, F3, F4, F8, F10, given, construct]

## Statement

Let $I=[a,b]$ with $a<b$, let $m,n\ge0$, and let $f,w\in C(I,\mathbb R)$
with $w>0$ on $I$. A best rational approximant in
$\mathcal R_{m,n}^+(I)$ exists and is unique. For a candidate $r=p/q$ with
positive weighted error $E_r:=\|w(f-r)\|_{\infty,I}>0$, let
$N=N_{m,n}(r)=m+n-d_{m,n}(r)$. Then $r$ is best if and only if there are
$N+2$ ordered nodes $x_0<\cdots<x_{N+1}$ in $I$ and
$\sigma\in\{-1,1\}$ such that

## Statement

Let $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let $(\Xi,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ be a
probability space, let $A\in F^{m\times n}$ be fixed, let $\ell\ge1$ be an
integer, and let $q\ge0$ be an integer. Let $\Omega:\Xi\to F^{n\times\ell}$
be measurable and let $P:\Xi\to F^{m\times m}$ be a measurable orthogonal
projector-valued map whose value $P(\xi)$ projects onto the output range of the procedure in
[[alg-randomized-power-subspace-iteration-with-qr]] applied to $A,\Omega(\xi),q$.
Assume
$$\mathbb E\|(I-P)(AA^*)^qA\|_2<\infty,$$
where expectation is with respect to $\mathbb P$. Then
$$\mathbb E\|(I-P)A\|_2\le \left(\mathbb E\|(I-P)(AA^*)^qA\|_2\right)^{1/(2q+1)}.$$
This is a transfer inequality; it assumes the powered error expectation has
already been bounded.

1.1 For each $\xi$, write $S_0=\operatorname{Ran}(A\Omega(\xi))$. At iteration $j$, the intermediate range is $A^*S_{j-1}$ and the next output range is $AA^*S_{j-1}$, because replacing a matrix by an orthonormal basis of its range preserves that range. Induction gives $\operatorname{Ran}(Q_q)=S_q=\operatorname{Ran}((AA^*)^qA\Omega(\xi))$, so its projector is the $P(\xi)$ in the statement. [given, F1, algebra]

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and neutral finite point-source data
$(A,V,\Lambda,\kappa_k,(x_i,q_i)_{i=1}^n)$ from
[[def-ewald-three-dimensional-periodic-source-data]], with pairwise distinct
source positions in $\mathbb T_A$. For $\alpha>0$ put
$$\sigma_k=\sum_iq_i e^{-i\kappa_k\cdot x_i},\qquad c_k(\alpha)=\frac{4\pi}{V|\kappa_k|^2}e^{-|\kappa_k|^2/(4\alpha^2)}\quad(k\ne0).$$
For every off-source point $x\notin\bigcup_i(x_i+\Lambda)$, the absolutely
convergent Ewald potential
$$U_\alpha(x)=\sum_iq_i\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda} \frac{\operatorname{erfc}(\alpha|x-x_i+\lambda|)}{|x-x_i+\lambda|} +\frac{4\pi}{V}\sum_{k\ne0}\frac{e^{-|\kappa_k|^2/(4\alpha^2)}}{|\kappa_k|^2} \sigma_k e^{i\kappa_k\cdot x}$$
is the off-source representative of the unique mean-zero periodic solution of
$-\Delta u=4\pi\rho$. Hence it is independent of $\alpha$.

Define the regular part at $x_i$ by
$$\operatorname{FP}_{x_i}U_\alpha= \lim_{x\to x_i}\left(U_\alpha(x)-\frac{q_i}{|x-x_i|}\right).$$
The limit exists, is independent of $\alpha$, and the renormalized energy is
$$E=\frac12\sum_iq_i\operatorname{FP}_{x_i}U_\alpha =\frac12\sum_i\sum_{(j,\lambda)\ne(i,0)}q_iq_j \frac{\operatorname{erfc}(\alpha|x_i-x_j+\lambda|)} {|x_i-x_j+\lambda|} +\frac12\sum_{k\ne0}c_k(\alpha)|\sigma_k|^2 -\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt\pi}\sum_iq_i^2.$$
The prime-exclusion written as $(j,\lambda)\ne(i,0)$ omits only each particle's
own zero-image singularity.

1.2 Define $S_\alpha(x)=\sum_iq_i\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\phi_s(|x-x_i+\lambda|)$ and $L_\alpha(x)=\frac{4\pi}{V}\sum_{k\ne0}\frac{e^{-|\kappa_k|^2/(4\alpha^2)}}{|\kappa_k|^2}\sigma_k e^{i\kappa_k\cdot x}$. The finitely many nonzero modes with $|\kappa_k|<1$ cause no difficulty, and [F4] bounds the remaining Gaussian shells; with $|\sigma_k|\le Q$, the reciprocal series is absolutely and uniformly convergent. Thus termwise integration over the finite-volume cell is valid, and [F10] gives $\frac1V\int_F L_\alpha(x)\,dx=\frac{4\pi}{V}\sum_{k\ne0}\frac{e^{-|\kappa_k|^2/(4\alpha^2)}}{|\kappa_k|^2}\sigma_k\left(\frac1V\int_F e^{i\kappa_k\cdot x}\,dx\right)=0$. For the real part, [F4], [F5], and Tonelli [F8] give $\int_F\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\phi_s(|x-x_i+\lambda|)\,dx =\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\operatorname{erfc}(\alpha|y|)}{|y|}\,dy =4\pi\int_0^\infty r\operatorname{erfc}(\alpha r)\,dr =\frac{\pi}{\alpha^2}.$ For the last equality, set $s=\alpha r$ and use the tail identity in [F1]. Tonelli [F8] gives $\int_0^\infty s\operatorname{erfc}(s)ds =\frac2{\sqrt\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-t^2}\left(\int_0^t s\,ds\right)dt =\frac1{\sqrt\pi}\int_0^\infty t^2e^{-t^2}dt.$ Integration by parts [F7] on $[0,R]$ gives $\int_0^R t^2e^{-t^2}dt=-Re^{-R^2}/2+(1/2)\int_0^R e^{-t^2}dt$; the boundary term tends to zero since $e^{R^2}\ge R^4/2$ for $R>0$. Taking $R\to\infty$ and using [F6] yields $\int_0^\infty t^2e^{-t^2}dt=\sqrt\pi/4$, so $\int_0^\infty s\operatorname{erfc}(s)ds=1/4$. Multiplying by $4\pi\alpha^{-2}$ gives the displayed value. Hence $\int_FS_\alpha=(\pi/\alpha^2)\sum_iq_i=0$, and $S_\alpha+L_\alpha$ has mean zero. [given, F1, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, F10, algebra]

4.1 The sum $U_\alpha=S_\alpha+L_\alpha$ is a mean-zero periodic distribution solution by steps 3.1 and 1.2. Uniqueness [F3] makes it equal to the same Fourier distribution $u$ for every $\alpha>0$. Its absolutely convergent representative is continuous off-source by step 2.1. If two such representatives differed at a point, one real or imaginary component of their difference would keep a strict sign on a small ball; choose a nonnegative smooth bump supported there using [F9]. Their distribution pairings with that bump would differ, contradicting equality to $u$. Thus the displayed potential is independent of $\alpha$. [A1, F3, F9, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 1.2]

## Statement

$(A,V,\Lambda,\kappa_k,(x_i,q_i)_{i=1}^n)$ from

source positions in $\mathbb T_A$. For $\alpha>0$ put
$$\sigma_k=\sum_iq_i e^{-i\kappa_k\cdot x_i},\qquad c_k(\alpha)=\frac{4\pi}{V|\kappa_k|^2}e^{-|\kappa_k|^2/(4\alpha^2)}\quad(k\ne0).$$
For every off-source point $x\notin\bigcup_i(x_i+\Lambda)$, the absolutely
convergent Ewald potential
$$U_\alpha(x)=\sum_iq_i\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda} \frac{\operatorname{erfc}(\alpha|x-x_i+\lambda|)}{|x-x_i+\lambda|} +\frac{4\pi}{V}\sum_{k\ne0}\frac{e^{-|\kappa_k|^2/(4\alpha^2)}}{|\kappa_k|^2} \sigma_k e^{i\kappa_k\cdot x}$$
is the off-source representative of the unique mean-zero periodic solution of
$-\Delta u=4\pi\rho$. Hence it is independent of $\alpha$.

Define the regular part at $x_i$ by
$$\operatorname{FP}_{x_i}U_\alpha= \lim_{x\to x_i}\left(U_\alpha(x)-\frac{q_i}{|x-x_i|}\right).$$
The limit exists, is independent of $\alpha$, and the renormalized energy is
$$E=\frac12\sum_iq_i\operatorname{FP}_{x_i}U_\alpha =\frac12\sum_i\sum_{(j,\lambda)\ne(i,0)}q_iq_j \frac{\operatorname{erfc}(\alpha|x_i-x_j+\lambda|)} {|x_i-x_j+\lambda|} +\frac12\sum_{k\ne0}c_k(\alpha)|\sigma_k|^2 -\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt\pi}\sum_iq_i^2.$$
The prime-exclusion written as $(j,\lambda)\ne(i,0)$ omits only each particle's
own zero-image singularity.

1.2 Define $S_\alpha(x)=\sum_iq_i\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\phi_s(|x-x_i+\lambda|)$ and $L_\alpha(x)=\frac{4\pi}{V}\sum_{k\ne0}\frac{e^{-|\kappa_k|^2/(4\alpha^2)}}{|\kappa_k|^2}\sigma_k e^{i\kappa_k\cdot x}$. The finitely many nonzero modes with $|\kappa_k|<1$ cause no difficulty, and [F4] bounds the remaining Gaussian shells; with $|\sigma_k|\le Q$, the reciprocal series is absolutely and uniformly convergent. Thus termwise integration over the finite-volume cell is valid, and [F10] gives $\frac1V\int_F L_\alpha(x)\,dx=\frac{4\pi}{V}\sum_{k\ne0}\frac{e^{-|\kappa_k|^2/(4\alpha^2)}}{|\kappa_k|^2}\sigma_k\left(\frac1V\int_F e^{i\kappa_k\cdot x}\,dx\right)=0$. 2.1 On compact sets avoiding all source images, the real sum and each differentiated tail converge uniformly by the $\operatorname{erfc}$ bounds of [F1] and the shell controller [F4]. The reciprocal series and every derivative converge uniformly because each derivative adds only a fixed power of $|\kappa_k|$ to a Gaussian tail. Thus both are continuous off-source, periodic, and their Fourier operations below are legitimate. [F1, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

## Statement

Assume the collision-free exact-arithmetic branch of [[alg-planar-laplace-fmm-fixed-order]] with order $p\ge1$. For each target $i$ in leaf $D_i$, let $\mathcal F_i=\{(C,D)\in\mathcal F:i\in I_D\}$ be its far cell interactions. For $(C,D)\in\mathcal F_i$ put $R_{CD}=|c_D-c_C|$, $\rho_{CD}=(a_C+a_D)/R_{CD}<1$, and $Q_C=\sum_{j\in I_C}|q_j|$. If $u_i$ is the exact fixed-branch logarithmic potential and $\widetilde u_i$ the algorithm output, then
$$|u_i-\widetilde u_i|\le\sum_{(C,D)\in\mathcal F_i}\frac{Q_C\rho_{CD}^{p+1}}{(p+1)(1-\rho_{CD})}.$$
If $g_i=\sum_{j\ne i}q_j/(z_i-z_j)$ and $\widetilde g_i$ is the algorithm's complex derivative output, then
$$|g_i-\widetilde g_i|\le\sum_{(C,D)\in\mathcal F_i}\frac{Q_C}{R_{CD}}\frac{\rho_{CD}^{p}}{1-\rho_{CD}}.$$
Near interactions are exact. The second estimate is branch-independent; no floating-point rounding error is included.

2.2 Differentiate the convergent series with respect to $x$. The derivative of its degree-$m$ term is $(-1)^{m+1}(x-y_j)^{m-1}/D_0^m$, whose absolute value is at most $(|x|+|y_j|)^{m-1}/R^m\le \rho^{m-1}/R$. The series and its derivative converge uniformly on the smaller closed disk $|x|\le a_D$ because $\rho<1$, so termwise differentiation is valid. Summing the omitted degrees bounds the interaction derivative error by $Q_C R^{-1}\sum_{m=p+1}^{\infty}\rho^{m-1}=Q_C R^{-1}\rho^p/(1-\rho)$. The derivative of any additive branch constant is zero. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

## Statement

For the single-cluster evaluator of [[alg-three-dimensional-laplace-cluster-expansion]], let $Q=\sum_{j\in J}|q_j|$. If a target satisfies $r=|x-c|>a$, then its potential error obeys
$$|U(x)-\widetilde U_p(x)|\le\frac{Q}{r}\frac{(a/r)^{p+1}}{1-a/r}.$$
If a target region is contained in a ball of radius $b$ centered at $d$, with $R=|d-c|>a+b$, then every target in the region has error at most
$$\frac{Q}{R-b}\frac{\bigl(a/(R-b)\bigr)^{p+1}}{1-a/(R-b)}.$$
Let $S=|J|$ and let $T_0$ be the number of targets. Under the monomial-coefficient evaluation convention of the algorithm, forming moments and evaluating the truncated field costs $O((S+T_0)(p+1)^4)$ arithmetic operations after the basis coefficient arrays have been prepared. If all basis values at sources and targets are supplied, the coefficient accumulation and expansion evaluation alone cost $O((S+T_0)(p+1)^2)$. This is a single-cluster estimate; it is not a 3D multilevel FMM tree complexity theorem.

Applying the generating identity and then the addition identity in [F2] with ratio $r_j/r<1$ gives $\frac1{|x-y_j|}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}\frac{r_j^\ell}{r^{\ell+1}}P_\ell(\omega\cdot\omega_j)=4\pi\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2\ell+1}\frac{r_j^\ell}{r^{\ell+1}}\sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell}Y_{\ell m}(\omega)\overline{Y_{\ell m}(\omega_j)}$. For $r_j=0$, the same formula follows by the limit: the degree-zero term is $1/r$ and all positive-degree regular solid harmonics vanish at the center. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

## Statement

Fix $0<\delta\le\pi/2$ and $z\in\mathbb C$ with $\operatorname{Re}z>0$.
For the branch $\ell_+$ from [[def-loggamma-right-halfplane-branch]],
[[lem-binet-loggamma-right-halfplane-identity]] gives

## Statement

In one dimension, let $g_i(x_A,a)=x_A^ie^{-ax_A^2}$ and $g_j(x_B,b)=x_B^je^{-bx_B^2}$, with $x_A=x-A$, $x_B=x-B$, $p=a+b$, $P=(aA+bB)/p$, and $K=e^{-ab(A-B)^2/p}$. There are unique coefficients $E_{ij}^t$ such that
$$g_i(x_A,a)g_j(x_B,b)=\sum_{t=0}^{i+j}E_{ij}^t\Lambda_t(x;p,P).$$
With $E_{00}^0=K$ and $E_{ij}^t=0$ outside $0\le t\le i+j$, they satisfy
$$E_{i+1,j}^t=\frac{E_{ij}^{t-1}}{2p}+(P-A)E_{ij}^t+(t+1)E_{ij}^{t+1},$$
$$E_{i,j+1}^t=\frac{E_{ij}^{t-1}}{2p}+(P-B)E_{ij}^t+(t+1)E_{ij}^{t+1}.$$
In three dimensions the pair expansion is the product of the three one-dimensional expansions, so it is a finite sum of $\Lambda_{tuv}$ with $0\le t\le\alpha_1+\beta_1$, $0\le u\le\alpha_2+\beta_2$, and $0\le v\le\alpha_3+\beta_3$.

1.1 Differentiating [F2] once gives $\Lambda_{t+1}=2p\,\partial_P^t((x-P)e^{-p(x-P)^2})$. The product rule applied $t$ times gives $\partial_P^t((x-P)h)=(x-P)\partial_P^th-t\partial_P^{t-1}h$, hence $$ (x-P)\Lambda_t=\frac{\Lambda_{t+1}}{2p}+t\Lambda_{t-1},$$ with the last term zero for $t=0$. [given, F2, algebra, induction, L9]

2.1 The polynomial factors $x_A^ix_B^j$ have degree at most $i+j$. By [F1] they multiply a common Gaussian. The polynomial part of $\Lambda_t$ has degree $t$ and leading coefficient $(2p)^t$, as follows inductively from $\Lambda_{t+1}=2p(x-P)\Lambda_t-2pt\Lambda_{t-1}$. Thus these polynomials form a triangular basis of the polynomials of degree at most $i+j$, which gives existence and uniqueness of the finite coefficients $E_{ij}^t$. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra, induction]

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice, every edge component is anchored, each $\kappa_e$ is constant with
$0<\kappa_{\min}\le\kappa_e\le\kappa_{\max}$, and the weak solution $u$ of
[[thm-metric-graph-weak-elliptic-problem]] satisfies
$u_e\in H^2(0,\ell_e)$, as defined in
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], on every edge. For the conforming P1 space $V_h$ of
[[def-metric-graph-p1-edge-mesh]], let $u_h\in V_h$ solve
$$a(u_h,v_h)=F(v_h)\qquad(v_h\in V_h),$$
where $a$ and $F$ are the weak diffusion form and load of that theorem. Put
$L_\Gamma=\sum_e\ell_e$,
$M_a=\kappa_{\max}$, and

## Statement

On the periodic staggered grid of
[[def-na-periodic-staggered-grid-stokes-operators]], every admissible backward-
Euler step of [[alg-na-periodic-incremental-pressure-correction]] and every
admissible BDF2 step of
[[alg-na-bdf2-incremental-and-rotational-pressure-correction]] has a unique
predictor, a unique mean-zero pressure increment, and a unique updated pair.
Both algorithms preserve the zero-mean pressure gauge and exact discrete
incompressibility.

1.1 For any nonzero $v\in V_h$, the componentwise Laplacian definition and finite periodic reindexing give $$ (A_hv,v)_{M_h}=h^{d-2}\sum_{i,\ell,j}|v_{i,j+e_\ell}-v_{i,j}|^2\ge0. $$ Therefore $( (I+k\nu A_h)v,v)_{M_h}=\|v\|_{M_h}^2+k\nu(A_hv,v)_{M_h}>0$. ## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and the setup of [[def-crouzeix-raviart-face-average-interpolant]], a
shape-regular affine mesh, and $1/2<r\le1$. The face-average interpolant is
defined for every $u\in H^{1+r}(K)$ by the traces of
[[lem-crouzeix-raviart-simplex-traces-and-green-identity]] and reproduces
$\mathbb P_1(K)$. Uniformly over all cells,
$$\|\nabla(u-I_K^{CR}u)\|_{L^2(K)} \le C h_K^r|u|_{H^{1+r}(K)},\qquad \|u-I_K^{CR}u\|_{L^2(K)} \le C h_K^{1+r}|u|_{H^{1+r}(K)}.$$
For each facet $F\subset\partial K$,
$$h_F^{-1/2}\|\gamma_F(u-I_K^{CR}u)\|_{L^2(F)} \le C h_K^r|u|_{H^{1+r}(K)}.$$
If $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then the global interpolant has matching interior
face means and zero boundary face means, so $I_h^{CR}u\in V_h^{CR,0}$.

1.1 On the reference simplex, each face mean of $v\in H^1$ is bounded by $C\|v\|_{H^1}$ by [F2]. The interpolant is a finite sum of these means times fixed affine shape polynomials, so it is bounded from $H^1$ to $H^1$. The trace-defined formula of [[def-crouzeix-raviart-face-average-interpolant]] is therefore continuous on $H^{1+r}\subset H^1$. [A1, F2, given]

2.1 First work on the reference simplex. Choose an affine polynomial $p$ with $
abla p=\operatorname{avg}_K
abla u$ and $\operatorname{avg}_K(u-p)=0$. For $1/2<r<1$, applying the fractional Poincare estimate proved in step 1.1 of [[lem-crouzeix-raviart-simplex-traces-and-green-identity]] to each component of $
abla u$ gives $\|
abla(u-p)\|_{L^2(K)}\le C|u|_{H^{1+r}(K)}$. The mean-zero Poincare–Wirtinger inequality [F3] then gives $\|u-p\|_{L^2(K)}\le C\|
abla(u-p)\|_{L^2(K)}$. At $r=1$, apply [F3] to the mean-zero first derivatives, then again to $u-p$, obtaining $\|u-p\|_{H^1(K)}\le C|u|_{H^2(K)}$. [A1, F3, given, step 1.1]
